options.B: Recommend The Hancock Line — every county in Maine kept whole, bought by leaving the two districts unequal

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4
protagonist: Margo Thibodeau, senior staff analyst to Maine's apportionment commission

deliverables.text: A map-space count: the Fundamental Counting Principle total for assigning Maine's counties to two districts, plus a size-breakdown row of binomial coefficients with at least four computed by hand and the row shown to sum to the FCP total.

A recursion sheet: (a) a recursive formula with its base case for the assignment count at k counties; (b) a recursive formula with base cases for the size-breakdown row, each entry built from two entries of the previous row; (c) the conversion of (a) into an explicit closed formula, checked against the D1 total.

An exhaustiveness certificate: a proof by mathematical induction that the size-breakdown row sums to the explicit total for every k, with base case and inductive step written as separately labeled parts and the line where the D2(b) recursion is used named explicitly.

A pigeonhole brief: three claims proved by the Pigeonhole Principle with no plan enumerated — at least one district at or above the ideal (so exact equality is impossible for Maine), at least half the counties (rounded up) in one district, and at least two of the four largest counties in one district with the population consequence stated.

A scorecard for The Kennebec Split against The Hancock Line: county-line crossings with the crossed borders named, each plan's district populations and BOTH deviation figures — the largest district's distance from the ideal and the maximum deviation (larger minus smaller) — in people and converted to a percent of the ideal, the number of Mainers in a divided county, and a recommendation set against the court standard in Appendix E, including one sentence on why the half-size figure is not comparable to Appendix E's percentages.

balance.argument_a: The Kennebec Split wins both numbers on the board. Its two districts differ by 1 person — the minimum arithmetically available to Maine, since 1,362,359 is odd — against The Hancock Line's 3,765; as maximum deviation that is 0.000147% against 0.5527%. It also wins the case's own primary metric, 10 county-line crossings to 11. Karcher is the authority that bites: there are no de minimis population variations which could practicably be avoided, and A is standing proof that B's 3,765 could have been avoided. The price is one divided county, and only 53,595 of Kennebec's 123,642 residents sit on the short side of the cut.
balance.argument_b: The Hancock Line divides none of Maine's 16 counties and leaves all 123,642 Kennebec residents with a single member of Congress instead of splitting them 53,595 / 70,047. Its 0.5527% maximum deviation sits below both Appendix E benchmarks — under the 0.6984% struck down in Karcher and under the 0.79% upheld in Tennant — and Tennant upheld that larger figure on exactly the justification B is buying: not splitting political subdivisions is a valid, neutral state districting policy. The single crossing B concedes is not a border at all; it is MA1's invented weight for severing Kennebec. Price that severance at 2 and the plans tie at 11; price it higher and B wins outright.
balance.margin_basis: County-line crossings for The Kennebec Split (9 borders along + 1 severance weight = 10) against The Hancock Line (11 borders along, no severance = 11), computed in sensitivity_model.py from the Appendix B county adjacency list, the Appendix A county populations and the Appendix H MA1/MA2/MA5 conventions. Margin = (higher - lower) / lower = 10.0%.
balance.twist_effect: A commissioner moves from the floor to strike the MA3 shortlist rule and substitute Oxford County for Hancock as the whole-county plan. Oxford runs along 9 borders and through none, so the whole-county side wins the primary metric 9 to 10 — an 11.11% margin the other way, and evaluate_twist() flips the winner from A to B. At the same time Oxford's maximum deviation is 8,363 people, 1.2277%, above both the 0.79% upheld in Tennant and the 0.6984% struck down in Karcher. Both popular positions break at once: 'A wins the rubric as well' dies for the A side and 'our plan is the legally comfortable one' dies for the B side, and the residue is that Margo's rubric and Margo's shortlist rule recommend different plans.
balance.stability_note: Margin 10.0% (A wins). MA1 flexed +/-50% by probe 5: 15.8% at weight 0.5, 4.8% at weight 1.5 — the ranking does not move, and the two plans tie only at weight 2. Two non-numeric conventions cannot be swept by probe 5 and are therefore stated in the open in Appendix H and in FACILITATOR.md. MA2: counting Kennebec in the southern district raises A to 12, so B wins by 9.1% — the winner flips but both readings stay inside SPEC section 2's 20% cap. MA5: excluding the Hancock-Knox water boundary drops A to 9 while B stays at 11, widening the margin to 22.2%, past the cap and in A's favour. A guide must not defend 10.0% as convention-free.

facilitator.twist: A commissioner has moved from the floor to strike the staff shortlist rule and swap Oxford County in for Hancock. Look at Appendix D again with that motion in front of you: the Oxford version splits the state 685,361 against 676,998. It runs along 9 county borders and through none, so it beats The Kennebec Split's 10 on Margo's own rubric by 11.11%. And its maximum deviation is 8,363 people, 1.2277% — larger than the 0.79% the Court upheld in Tennant and larger than the 0.6984% it struck down in Karcher. The whole-county plan is now the best plan on Margo's rubric and the only plan on the table that might not survive a court. Sixty seconds: does that change your recommendation, or only your reason for it?
facilitator.trap: Primary: most Heroes will read Appendix F's 65,534 as a completed audit and write 'the commission examined every plan' straight into the pitch, when nothing in the packet examines anything — 65,534 counts how many plans exist, not evidence that any were checked, and only the D3 induction proof licenses the claim. Second: quoting one district's distance from the ideal (half-size — 1,882.5 people, 0.2764%, for The Hancock Line) against Karcher's and Tennant's maximum-deviation percentages. Harmless on the two plans on the table and decisive at the twist, where it turns Oxford's 1.2277% into 0.6139% and reverses the legal conclusion.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Weight of a county the district line runs through, in county-line crossings
modeling_assumptions.basis: No published redistricting rubric assigns a numeric weight to severing a county. The case fixes one so that a plan that severs a county and a plan that does not can be compared in a single figure.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The dial that decides the primary metric. The Kennebec Split scores 9 borders plus this weight; The Hancock Line scores 11 and pays no weight, so the two tie at weight 2 — below 2 A scores better, above 2 B does. Flexed +/-50% in Tier 2 probe 5 (0.5 and 1.5): the ranking does not move (15.8% and 4.8%).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: For the border count, a divided county is assigned to whichever district holds more of its people
modeling_assumptions.value_used: majority assignment — Kennebec counted in the northern district (70,047 > 53,595)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Without a rule, 'which borders does the line run along' has no answer for a divided county, because the answer depends on which of its towns sit where — town-level geography this case does not model. Majority assignment is the convention an analyst reaches for first.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Load-bearing: it decides who wins. Counting Kennebec in the southern district instead raises The Kennebec Split to 12 and The Hancock Line wins the primary metric by 9.1% where the stated margin is 10.0% the other way. Both readings stay inside SPEC section 2's cap, so the case is close either way — but the winner is a convention, not a fact. Not a numeric dial, so probe 5 cannot sweep it; stated in the open here and in balance.stability_note.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Staff shortlist rule: keep the five southern counties together, then add either one whole county or part of one county, choosing the option whose two districts come closest to equal population
modeling_assumptions.value_used: applied to Appendix D; it is what put Hancock rather than Oxford on the table
modeling_assumptions.basis: Continuity of representation — holding down how many Mainers change members of Congress — is a real redistricting criterion, and equal population is the one constraint a congressional plan cannot trade away. Together they are how these two plans and no others reached the shortlist. It is staff practice, not statute.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Directly load-bearing on which plans are on the table at all. Score Appendix D on crossings instead and Oxford, not Hancock, is Option B — a plan whose districts differ by 8,363 people, 1.2277%, above both Appendix E benchmarks. The twist is a floor motion to do exactly that.

modeling_assumptions.value_used: Margo Thibodeau, the staff room and the choice between exactly these two plans are invented
modeling_assumptions.basis: Maine's commission, its September 27, 2021 report to the Legislature [S7], the enacted plan [S5] and every number in the case are real. The internal deliberation is not, and no record says The Hancock Line was ever proposed.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: None on the arithmetic. It does mean 'what the commission actually decided' is not evidence about what it should have decided.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: A water boundary counts as a county-line border, exactly like a land boundary
modeling_assumptions.value_used: all 34 Appendix B borders counted, including Hancock-Knox
modeling_assumptions.basis: The Census county adjacency file [S4] makes no distinction between land and water boundaries, and inventing one would need a rule about how much water is too much — a rule this case has no source for. Taking the published file as published is the choice that can be checked, and it is also the working convention: redistricting analysts and the GIS tools that support them (including the Bureau's own Redistricting Data Program) use the published county adjacency layer as the definition of "neighbor," water crossings included, rather than re-deriving one county by county from travel distance. RESOLVED 2026-08-18: this is the case's committed convention on its own real-world merits, not a choice made to keep the margin under SPEC section 2's cap -- see case.json.qa.note and QA_REPORT.md for the full reasoning.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The Kennebec Split's line runs along Hancock-Knox; The Hancock Line's does not. Excluding that one border drops A to 9 while B stays at 11, widening the margin from 10.0% to 22.2% — past SPEC section 2's cap, in A's favour. The ranking does not flip but the case stops being close. Non-numeric, so probe 5 cannot sweep it; stated here and in balance.stability_note.

sensitivity_note: Redistricting is politically charged in a way that has nothing to do with the math in this case. The case is built entirely on population counts, county borders and case law; it uses no election results and no party registration, and neither option is a partisan position. If a learner steers the discussion toward parties or candidates, redirect to the two numbers on the table — crossings and deviation — and note that both plans satisfy the same legal criteria (and note that the two Supreme Court decisions in Appendix E are genuinely contested against each other — the case does not pretend they point the same way).

cohort_bands.note: Socratic plan and anchor timings run as written in FACILITATOR.md (0:00-45:00). Anchor 1 is a real show-of-hands split; all three deep-conflict threads run; the D3 induction proof gets its own board walk-through during the Data Deep Dive.

Anchors 2 and 3 combine into one pass ('what are we actually counting, and how would we check it'). Run only one deep-conflict thread (whose harm is bigger) at 20:00-30:00. The twist still drops at 15:00. Total runtime about half. Present the D3 induction proof as a completed artifact to critique rather than deriving it live.

No vote to take at Anchor 1 — the learner states an initial position instead. The guide argues the other side directly rather than cold-calling. Skip the deep-conflict threads; go from the twist recommit straight to Close. Ask the learner to read their own induction proof aloud line by line, which is where a one-on-one has an advantage over a room.

Solver chose A, named its optimized metric (maximum population deviation as a percent of the ideal, deliberately not the crossings proxy, reasoning explicitly that crossings flips under the opposite MA2 convention -- exactly the sensitivity the case discloses), showed correct arithmetic for both plans, answered all 7 required questions, and additionally: (a) correctly derived Appendix F's now-redacted FCP total via 2^16=65,536 / 65,534 non-empty, from the county list alone, and explained what the count does and does not prove; (b) correctly applied D4(iii)'s now-explicit guaranteed-minimum method, computing Penobscot+Kennebec=275,841 as the floor and explicitly rejecting Cumberland+York=515,041 as not guaranteed. qa.note: TIER2_PASS, all six probes recorded, 0 FAIL, 0 open author decisions remaining as of 2026-08-18. All three items in the prior note are now resolved, not merely disclosed: (1) MA5 water-boundary convention -- decided FINAL as 'counted' (all 34 Appendix B borders, including Hancock-Knox) on its own real-world merits: this matches the working professional convention (redistricting analysts and their GIS tooling, including the Census Bureau's own Redistricting Data Program, treat the published county adjacency file as the definition of 'neighbor' without hand-excluding water crossings, because doing so would require an unsourced threshold rule for how much water is 'too much'). Under this convention margin_pct stays 10.0%, inside SPEC section 2's ~20% cap -- no retuning was needed because the defensible reading and the in-cap reading are the same reading here. The alternate reading (water boundaries excluded, A drops to 9, margin widens to 22.2%, past the cap) is retained as a disclosed sensitivity finding in balance.stability_note, Appendix B, Appendix H MA5 and FACILITATOR.md -- a real, legitimate classroom challenge a Hero can raise, but not the case's own committed convention, and not something case-write or case-readiness picked in order to dodge the cap. (2) Appendix F no longer prints 65,536/65,534 -- case.md now requires the Hero to derive the Fundamental Counting Principle total from Appendix A's county list (D1's own deliverable), matching the six-degrees-of-exposure repair pattern of disclosing enough surrounding data for real, checkable derivation rather than printing the answer. This makes FACILITATOR.md's primary trap ('a count is not an audit') strictly stronger, not weaker: a Hero who does the honest work of deriving the count is, if anything, more likely to mistake their own derivation for an audit, which is exactly the misconception D3's induction proof exists to correct. Re-confirmed by the 2026-08-18 fresh P1 solve, which derived 65,536/65,534 correctly and unprompted. (3) D4(iii)'s method is now stated explicitly in case.md: the population consequence must be reported as the guaranteed minimum (the smallest population pair among Maine's four largest counties), because Pigeonhole proves existence of a pair but not which pair, so only the floor sum is an assertion the principle actually licenses. This is the reading FACILITATOR.md already treated as correct pre-fix (Penobscot+Kennebec=275,841, not the vivid but unguaranteed Cumberland+York=515,041); it is now unambiguous in the student-facing text rather than left to the guide to catch after the fact. Re-confirmed by the fresh P1 solve, which applied the specified method correctly and explicitly rejected the larger, non-guaranteed pairing.
